notes.definition: The main energy resources on Earth are fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves. A renewable energy resource is one that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used.
explanation: Energy resources are used for three main purposes: transport, electricity generation and heating. Fossil fuels (coal, oil and natural gas) and nuclear fuel (uranium or plutonium) are non-renewable: they are being used up faster than they can be replaced and will eventually run out. Bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, tidal, solar and wave resources are renewable because they are replenished as they are used.

For transport, most vehicles use petrol or diesel, which come from oil, although bio-fuels such as bioethanol and biodiesel can replace some of this, and electric vehicles use electricity from the National Grid. For heating, many homes burn natural gas or oil, or use electric heaters; renewable options include solar water heaters, burning wood (a bio-fuel) and geothermal heating in suitable areas. For electricity generation, power stations burn fossil fuels or bio-fuels, or use nuclear fuel, to make steam that turns turbines; wind, hydro-electric, tidal and wave power turn turbines directly, and solar cells transfer energy from sunlight to electricity.

Reliability matters because electricity demand must be met at all times. Fossil fuel and nuclear power stations are reliable: fuel can be stored and they can run whenever needed, although nuclear stations take a long time to start up. Gas stations can be started quickly to meet sudden demand. Hydro-electric and geothermal power are reliable, and tides are predictable, but wind, solar and wave power depend on the weather or time of day, so they are unreliable. Backup supplies or energy storage are needed when they are not available.

Every resource has environmental impacts. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which contributes to global warming and climate change; coal also releases sulfur dioxide, which causes acid rain, and oil can spill and harm wildlife. Nuclear power releases no carbon dioxide while running but produces radioactive waste that stays dangerous for a very long time, and accidents can be serious. Wind farms can be noisy and spoil the view; hydro-electric dams flood valleys and destroy habitats; tidal barrages affect estuary habitats; bio-fuel crops use land that could grow food.

Patterns of energy use change over time. In the UK, the use of coal for electricity has fallen sharply while renewable resources such as wind and solar have increased, because of concerns about climate change, government targets, and falling costs of renewable technology. Science can identify the environmental problems caused by energy resources, but it cannot always solve them alone: decisions also depend on political, social, ethical and economic factors, such as cost, public opinion, jobs and the security of energy supply.
keyFacts: Main resources: fossil fuels, nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, tides, the Sun and water waves.
Renewable: replenished as it is used. Non-renewable: will run out (fossil fuels, nuclear fuel).
Energy resources are used for transport, electricity generation and heating.
Fossil fuels and nuclear are reliable but non-renewable.
Wind, solar and waves are unreliable because they depend on the weather or time of day; tides are predictable.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, contributing to global warming and climate change.
Burning coal releases sulfur dioxide, which causes acid rain.
Nuclear power produces no carbon dioxide in operation but creates long-lasting radioactive waste.
UK use of coal has fallen and use of renewables has risen.
Decisions about energy also involve political, social, ethical and economic issues.

keyTerms.definition: A resource that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used, for example wind or solar.
A resource that is used up faster than it can be replaced and will eventually run out, for example coal or uranium.
Coal, oil and natural gas, formed over millions of years from the remains of living organisms.
A fuel made from plant or animal matter, such as wood, bioethanol or biodiesel.
How dependably a resource can supply energy whenever it is needed.
Energy from hot rocks underground, used to heat water to make steam or to heat buildings.
Describes a fuel whose use releases no more carbon dioxide than was absorbed when it was produced, as claimed for bio-fuels.

workedExamples.title: Calculating a share from data
workedExamples.question: In one year a country generated 160 TWh of electricity. 48 TWh came from wind. Calculate the percentage of electricity generated by wind.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a resource for a remote island
workedExamples.question: A small island with strong winds, no rivers and no fossil fuel reserves needs electricity. Evaluate using wind turbines with a diesel generator as backup.
steps: Wind turbines are suitable because the island is windy, and wind is renewable and releases no carbon dioxide while generating.
But wind is unreliable: on calm days the turbines produce little or no electricity.
A diesel generator is reliable and can be started quickly, so it can supply electricity when the wind is low.
However diesel is a fossil fuel that must be imported and releases carbon dioxide, so it should be used only as a backup.
Conclusion: the combination gives a reliable supply while keeping fuel use and emissions low.
workedExamples.answer: A good choice: wind provides most electricity renewably, while the diesel generator covers calm periods, so the supply is reliable.

workedExamples.title: Interpreting reliability data
workedExamples.question: A wind farm has a maximum output of 300 MW. Over a year its average output is 35% of the maximum. Calculate its average output and explain why it is less than the maximum.
steps: The output depends on wind speed, which varies; on calm days there is little output and in very strong winds turbines are shut down for safety.
So the average is much lower than the maximum.
workedExamples.answer: 105 MW; wind speed varies, so the turbines rarely produce their maximum output.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think nuclear fuel is renewable because it produces no carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.right: In fact nuclear fuel (uranium) is non-renewable: it is mined and will run out. Low emissions and renewability are different ideas.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think renewable resources have no environmental impact.
misconceptions.right: In fact they do: hydro-electric dams flood habitats, wind farms affect the landscape and bio-fuel crops take up farmland.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say tidal power is unreliable like wind.
misconceptions.right: In fact tides are predictable, so tidal power is reliable in timing, although output varies through the day.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the main problem with fossil fuels is only that they will run out.
misconceptions.right: In fact burning them also releases carbon dioxide (climate change) and sulfur dioxide (acid rain).

realWorld: The UK now generates a large share of its electricity from offshore wind farms, while its last coal-fired power station has closed.
Iceland uses geothermal energy from volcanic rocks to heat homes and generate electricity.
Pumped storage hydroelectric schemes, such as Dinorwig in Wales, can supply electricity within seconds when demand suddenly rises.
examTips: When asked to evaluate a resource, give advantages AND disadvantages, then a justified conclusion.
Be specific: say 'releases carbon dioxide, which contributes to global warming', not just 'it pollutes'.
Use the word 'reliable' with a reason, for example 'unreliable because it depends on the wind speed'.
In data questions, describe the trend with numbers from the data, then suggest reasons.
Remember that energy decisions involve cost, politics and public opinion, not only science.

questions.question: Which of these is a renewable energy resource?
markScheme: 1 mark: Wind
questions.explanation: Wind is replenished as it is used. Coal and gas are fossil fuels and nuclear fuel is mined uranium; all of these will run out.

questions.question: What is meant by a renewable energy resource?
options: A resource that is being replenished as it is used
A resource that releases no pollution
A resource that is always available
A resource that can be burned
markScheme: 1 mark: A resource that is being replenished as it is used
questions.explanation: Renewable means it is replaced naturally as quickly as it is used. Some renewables are not always available (wind) and some can be burned (bio-fuels).

questions.question: Which energy resource is non-renewable?
markScheme: 1 mark: Nuclear fuel
questions.explanation: Uranium is mined from the ground and the supply is limited, so it will eventually run out.

questions.question: For which purpose are petrol and diesel mainly used?
options: Generating most of the UK's electricity
markScheme: 1 mark: Transport
questions.explanation: Petrol and diesel are made from oil and power most cars, lorries and buses.

questions.question: Which renewable energy resource is the most predictable?
markScheme: 1 mark: Tidal
questions.explanation: Tides are caused by the Moon and happen at predictable times each day. Wind, solar and waves depend on the weather.

questions.question: Burning coal releases sulfur dioxide. What environmental problem does this cause?
markScheme: 1 mark: Acid rain
questions.explanation: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in water in the atmosphere, forming acid rain that damages trees, lakes and buildings. Carbon dioxide from coal contributes to climate change.

questions.question: Which is a disadvantage of hydro-electric power?
options: It releases large amounts of carbon dioxide when generating
Building the dam floods a valley, destroying habitats
markScheme: 1 mark: Building the dam floods a valley, destroying habitats
questions.explanation: Hydro-electric power is renewable, reliable and quick to start, and releases no carbon dioxide when generating, but the reservoir floods land.

questions.question: Bio-fuels are often described as carbon neutral. Why?
options: Burning them releases no carbon dioxide
The plants absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, balancing the carbon dioxide released when the fuel is burned
They are made from fossil fuels
They are only used in electric cars
markScheme: 1 mark: The plants absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, balancing the carbon dioxide released when the fuel is burned
questions.explanation: Bio-fuels do release carbon dioxide when burned, but the same amount was taken in by photosynthesis. In practice, farming and transport mean they are not completely carbon neutral.

questions.question: A country gets much of its electricity from wind. Why does it still keep some gas-fired power stations?
options: Gas power stations release no carbon dioxide
Gas power stations can be started quickly to meet demand when wind output is low
Gas power stations take a long time to start, so they provide a steady supply
markScheme: 1 mark: Gas power stations can be started quickly to meet demand when wind output is low
questions.explanation: Wind is unreliable, so a backup that can respond quickly is needed. Gas is non-renewable and releases carbon dioxide, but it has a short start-up time.

questions.question: Which is a disadvantage of generating electricity using nuclear fuel?
options: It produces radioactive waste that remains dangerous for a very long time
It releases large amounts of carbon dioxide while generating
It is unreliable because it depends on the weather
markScheme: 1 mark: It produces radioactive waste that remains dangerous for a very long time
questions.explanation: Nuclear power is reliable and releases no carbon dioxide while operating, but the waste must be stored safely for thousands of years.

questions.question: Which renewable energy resource can be used directly to fuel vehicles?
markScheme: 1 mark: Bio-fuel
questions.explanation: Bio-fuels such as bioethanol and biodiesel can be burned in vehicle engines. The other resources are used to generate electricity or for heating.

questions.question: In one year a country generated 320 TWh of electricity. 80 TWh came from wind. Calculate the percentage of the country's electricity that came from wind.
markScheme: 1 mark: 25%
questions.explanation: Percentage = part ÷ total × 100 = 80 ÷ 320 × 100 = 25%.

questions.question: A coal-fired power station has a maximum output of 2000 MW. Each wind turbine has a maximum output of 2.5 MW. Calculate how many wind turbines would be needed to match the maximum output of the power station.
markScheme: 1 mark: 800 turbines
questions.explanation: 2000 ÷ 2.5 = 800. In reality more would be needed, because turbines rarely produce their maximum output.

questions.question: A wind farm has a maximum power output of 300 MW. Over a year its average output is 35% of its maximum. Calculate its average power output.
markScheme: 1 mark: 105 MW
questions.explanation: 35% = 0.35, and 0.35 × 300 = 105 MW. The average is low because wind speed varies.

questions.question: A gas-fired power station supplies 1500 MW of electrical power. Its efficiency is 38%. Calculate the rate at which energy is transferred from the fuel (the total power input). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: efficiency = 0.38
1 mark: total input = 1500 ÷ 0.38 = 3947 MW
1 mark: 3950 MW (3 s.f.)
questions.explanation: Rearrange efficiency = useful output ÷ total input: total input = 1500 ÷ 0.38 = 3947 MW, about 3950 MW. Most of the fuel's energy is wasted heating the surroundings.

questions.question: Name two fossil fuels.
markScheme: 1 mark: any two from coal, oil, natural gas
questions.explanation: The three fossil fuels are coal, oil and natural gas, formed from the remains of ancient organisms.

questions.question: State the three main uses of energy resources.
markScheme: 2 marks: transport, electricity generation and heating
1 mark: any two of these
questions.explanation: AQA identifies transport, electricity generation and heating as the main uses.

questions.question: Name one renewable energy resource that can be used to heat homes directly.
markScheme: 1 mark: any one from solar (water heating), geothermal, bio-fuel such as wood
questions.explanation: Solar water heaters, geothermal heat pumps and wood burners all provide heating from renewable resources.

questions.question: Explain why solar cells are an unreliable source of electricity.
markScheme: 1 mark: they produce no electricity at night
1 mark: and less on cloudy days or in winter, so the output depends on weather and time
questions.explanation: Solar cells need sunlight; output varies unpredictably with cloud and falls to zero at night, so they cannot guarantee supply.

questions.question: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using nuclear power stations to generate electricity.
acceptedAnswers: lots of energy from small mass of fuel
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage, e.g. no carbon dioxide released while generating; reliable; a small mass of fuel gives a lot of energy
1 mark: disadvantage, e.g. radioactive waste; risk of serious accidents; high cost of building and decommissioning; non-renewable; slow start-up
questions.explanation: Nuclear is reliable and low-carbon, but waste, accident risk and cost are major drawbacks.

questions.question: Explain how burning fossil fuels contributes to climate change.
markScheme: 1 mark: burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas)
1 mark: which increases global warming, leading to climate change
questions.explanation: Extra carbon dioxide in the atmosphere increases the greenhouse effect, raising average global temperatures and changing the climate.

questions.question: Describe how geothermal energy can be used, and give one limitation.
markScheme: 1 mark: hot rocks underground heat water, which can be used to heat buildings or make steam to drive turbines
1 mark: limitation: only practical in a few places (e.g. volcanic areas) where hot rocks are near the surface, or high drilling costs
questions.explanation: Geothermal is reliable and renewable but is only economic where hot rocks are close to the surface, such as Iceland.

questions.question: The use of coal to generate electricity in the UK has fallen sharply in recent decades. Suggest three reasons for this.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any three: coal releases the most carbon dioxide per unit of energy, contributing to climate change; government targets or laws to cut emissions; renewable technology such as wind and solar has become cheaper; gas releases less carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide than coal; coal causes acid rain; public pressure; UK coal reserves are expensive to mine
questions.explanation: The decline is driven by environmental concerns and policy, plus economic changes that made gas and renewables more attractive.

questions.question: Scientists agree that wind farms reduce carbon dioxide emissions, yet some local communities oppose new wind farms. Suggest why scientific evidence alone cannot settle whether a wind farm should be built.
markScheme: 1 mark: local objections such as noise, spoiling the view, or effects on wildlife or property values
1 mark: the decision also depends on social, economic, political or ethical factors (such as cost, jobs or public opinion), not only scientific evidence
questions.explanation: Science can measure emissions and effects, but whether the benefits outweigh local costs is a value judgement involving people, money and politics.

questions.question:
A town's electricity currently comes from a coal-fired power station. The council proposes closing it and building an offshore wind farm instead.
Evaluate this proposal.
markScheme: Indicative content: advantages of wind: renewable, will not run out; no carbon dioxide released while generating, so less contribution to climate change; no sulfur dioxide so no acid rain; no fuel costs; offshore sites have stronger, more consistent wind and less visual impact; disadvantages of wind: unreliable, no output when wind is calm or too strong; needs backup (e.g. gas) or energy storage; high building cost; possible effects on marine wildlife and birds; coal: reliable and can meet demand on request, but non-renewable, releases carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide; conclusion: a justified judgement, e.g. wind is better for the environment but must be combined with a reliable backup or storage.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed evaluation comparing both resources, covering reliability and environmental impact, with a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some advantages and disadvantages of both resources, with a conclusion that is not fully justified.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or both resources with no conclusion.
questions.explanation: An evaluation needs both sides and a conclusion. The key trade-off is wind's environmental benefit against its unreliability.

questions.question: Compare tidal power and wave power as ways of generating electricity.
markScheme: Indicative content: similarities: both renewable; neither releases carbon dioxide while generating; both use the movement of sea water to turn turbines or generators; both have high set-up costs and can affect marine habitats; differences: tides are predictable and occur twice a day, so tidal power is more reliable; wave power depends on the weather (wind), so it is unreliable; tidal barrages can generate large amounts of power but alter estuary habitats and affect shipping; wave generators produce smaller amounts and can be damaged by storms.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least one similarity and one difference, clearly explained, including reliability.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple points about one or both resources without clear comparison.
questions.explanation: A comparison must state how the two are alike and how they differ. Reliability is the key difference: tides are predictable, waves are not.

questions.question:
The table shows the percentage of electricity generated from each source in one country.
Year 2000: coal 33%, gas 39%, nuclear 21%, renewables 3%, other 4%
Year 2020: coal 2%, gas 36%, nuclear 16%, renewables 43%, other 3%
Describe the trends shown and suggest reasons for them.
markScheme: Indicative content: coal fell sharply from 33% to 2%; renewables rose greatly from 3% to 43%; gas stayed roughly the same (39% to 36%); nuclear fell slightly (21% to 16%); reasons: concern about carbon dioxide emissions and climate change; government targets and policies; falling cost of wind and solar; closure of old coal and nuclear stations; gas kept as a reliable, quick-start backup for variable renewables.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): trends described using data from the table and at least two sensible reasons linked to the trends.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two trends described, or reasons given without data.
questions.explanation: Quote numbers when describing trends. The swap from coal to renewables reflects climate policy and cheaper renewables; gas remains because it is reliable.

questions.question: Most homes in the UK are heated by burning natural gas. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this, and suggest one renewable alternative.
markScheme: Indicative content: advantages of gas: reliable, available on demand; can be supplied through pipes to many homes; relatively cheap; quick to heat; disadvantages: non-renewable and will run out; burning releases carbon dioxide, contributing to climate change; price depends on world markets and supply security; renewable alternative: solar water heating, geothermal heat, or burning bio-fuel (wood); an alternative may be less reliable or more expensive to install.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear advantages and disadvantages of gas with a suitable renewable alternative.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant points with limited discussion.
questions.explanation: Gas is reliable and convenient but non-renewable and high-carbon. Renewable options exist but have their own limitations.
